title: Given a two-dimensional grid of land and water cells, count how many separate islands exist, where an island is land connected horizontally or vertically.
shortTitle: Count the Number of Islands (Grid DFS Flood Fill)
topicTitle: Determine whether a given integer is a power of two. Solve in O

s1_definition.profdef: Counting islands treats a grid as an implicit graph where each land cell is a node connected to its four orthogonal land neighbours. You scan every cell, and each time you encounter unvisited land you increment the island count and run a flood fill, a depth-first or breadth-first traversal, that marks the whole connected land region as visited so it is not counted again. The algorithm visits every cell a constant number of times, so it runs in time proportional to the grid size.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India plots fraudulent accounts on a grid map, where a filled cell is a flagged account and neighbouring flagged cells are part of the same coordinated ring. A clerk sweeps the map cell by cell. The first time she touches a flagged cell that she has not seen, she declares a new ring and then "colours in" every flagged cell reachable from it up, down, left, and right, so the whole blob is marked done. She continues sweeping, and each fresh untouched blob she finds is another ring. The final tally of blobs is the number of rings.
s1_definition.oneliner: Scan the grid; each unvisited land cell starts a new island and a flood fill sinks its whole connected region so it is counted once.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Counting islands treats a grid as an implicit graph where each land cell is a node connected to its four orthogonal land neighbours. You scan every cell, and each time you encounter unvisited land you increment the island count and run a flood fill, a depth-first or breadth-first traversal, that marks the whole connected land region as visited so it is not counted again. The algorithm visits every cell a constant number of times, so it runs in time proportional to the grid size.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India plots fraudulent accounts on a grid map, where a filled cell is a flagged account and neighbouring flagged cells are part of the same coordinated ring. A clerk sweeps the map cell by cell. The first time she touches a flagged cell that she has not seen, she declares a new ring and then "colours in" every flagged cell reachable from it up, down, left, and right, so the whole blob is marked done. She continues sweeping, and each fresh untouched blob she finds is another ring. The final tally of blobs is the number of rings.

**One line to remember:** Scan the grid; each unvisited land cell starts a new island and a flood fill sinks its whole connected region so it is counted once.

sections.s2_technical:
The central idea is that an island is a connected component in a graph whose nodes are land cells and whose edges join orthogonally adjacent land. Counting connected components is a classic traversal problem: start a traversal from each unvisited node, and the number of traversals you had to start is the number of components.

The outer loop visits every cell with two nested loops over rows and columns. When it finds a land cell that has not been visited, it increments the counter and launches a depth-first flood fill from that cell. The flood fill is a recursion that, at each land cell, marks it visited then recurses into the four neighbours up, down, left, and right. A common in-place trick is to overwrite visited land with water, for example `grid[r][c] = '0';`, which both marks it and avoids a separate visited array. The recursion must guard its bounds and stop at water: `if (r < 0 || r >= rows || c < 0 || c >= cols || grid[r][c] != '1') return;`.

The reason each new land cell found by the outer loop is exactly one new island is that the flood fill always consumes the entire connected region before the outer loop advances. So any land the outer loop later encounters must belong to a region not reachable from previous starts, meaning a genuinely separate island. Time is proportional to rows times columns because each cell is examined a bounded number of times, and the recursion depth can reach the size of the largest island.

A senior-level nuance is the choice between depth-first and breadth-first flood fill and the recursion-depth risk. Depth-first recursion is concise but can overflow the stack on a huge single island, so for very large grids I switch to an explicit stack or a breadth-first queue. The same pattern generalises to flood-fill paint tools, region labelling in image processing, and connected-component analysis, and it is equivalent to a union-find grouping of adjacent land.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's fraud analytics plots suspicious accounts on a spatial grid, and clusters of adjacent flagged cells represent coordinated fraud rings. The team needs the count of distinct rings to size its investigation effort. This is exactly counting connected components, which flood fill solves.

Problem 2 — Each ring must be counted exactly once no matter how large or oddly shaped it is, so once we start on a flagged cell we must consume the whole connected blob before looking for the next ring. The flood fill marking visited cells guarantees that.

In our mini-project we build a `FraudGridScanner` with a `countRings` method over a character grid where one is a flagged account and zero is clear. The demo scans a small grid with a few separate clusters and logs the ring count.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a four-by-five grid with a two-by-two block of flags in the top-left, a small L-shaped cluster on the right, and a single lone flag in the bottom row.

Step 1: The outer loop starts at row zero, column zero, which is flagged. We increment the ring count to one and flood fill. The fill marks the top-left cell visited, then spreads to its flagged neighbours, consuming the whole two-by-two block, turning all four cells to clear.

Step 2: The outer loop continues scanning row zero and row one. All the cells it passes in the top-left block are now clear, so it does not start a new ring there, which is exactly why each blob counts once.

Step 3: At row one, column four, it finds a flag. We increment the ring count to two and flood fill. The fill spreads down and left into the connected flags at row two, columns three and four, consuming that L-shaped cluster and clearing it.

Step 4: The outer loop keeps scanning. It passes the now-cleared right cluster without starting a new ring.

Step 5: At row three, column one, it finds the lone flag. We increment the ring count to three and flood fill, which marks just that single cell since it has no flagged neighbours.

Step 6: The loop finishes the grid with nothing left flagged. The final count is three distinct rings, each discovered once because the flood fill consumed every connected blob before the outer loop moved on.

```
[2026-10-26 23:30:01] INFO    Distinct fraud rings: 3
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  grid (1=flag):          scan order → flood fill each blob
  1 1 0 0 0
  1 1 0 0 1      blob A = top-left 2x2   → ring 1, sink
  0 0 0 1 1      blob B = right L-shape   → ring 2, sink
  0 1 0 0 0      blob C = lone cell       → ring 3, sink

  outer loop finds unvisited '1' → count++ → sink(4-dir DFS)
  total = 3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Counting islands treats the grid as an implicit graph where every land cell is a node joined to its four orthogonal land neighbours, and an island is a connected component. The algorithm is to scan every cell, and each time I find an unvisited land cell I increment the island count and run a flood fill that marks the whole connected region as visited. The number of times I had to start a fresh flood fill is the number of islands.

The flood fill is a depth-first recursion that, at each land cell, marks it visited and then recurses into its four neighbours, stopping at the grid edges and at water. A neat trick is to mark a visited cell by overwriting it with water in place, which avoids a separate visited array. The reason each land cell the outer loop discovers is exactly one new island is that the flood fill always consumes the entire connected region before the loop advances, so any land encountered later must belong to a genuinely separate region. The whole thing runs in time proportional to the number of cells because each cell is touched a bounded number of times.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in fraud analytics, where suspicious accounts are plotted on a spatial grid and clusters of adjacent flagged cells represent coordinated fraud rings. Counting the distinct rings let the team size its investigation effort, and the flood fill guaranteed each ring, however large or oddly shaped, was counted exactly once.

The senior-level point I make is about the depth-first recursion's stack risk. On a huge grid that is essentially one giant island, the recursion can be as deep as the number of cells and overflow the call stack, so for very large inputs I switch to an explicit stack or a breadth-first queue. I also note that this pattern is the same as flood-fill paint tools and region labelling in image processing, and it can equivalently be solved with union-find by grouping adjacent land, so I treat it as the canonical connected-components problem on a grid.
